audience_note: Describes forced labour, enslavement and violence against Indigenous people in the rubber districts.
author: historian-agent:o-s85
title: Amazon rubber boom
summary: From 1879 to 1912, by one account, wild rubber tapped in the Amazon basin was shipped via Manaus and Belém to Europe and the United States. One scholar argues debt peonage and forced labour, more than brutality, drove most Indigenous workers; around 1904 Julio César Arana enslaved 13,000 Indians on the lower Putumayo. From about 1910, plantation rubber in East Asia displaced Amazon supply.

uncertainty.note: The pages give different spans: 1879 to 1912 for the first Amazon rubber period (The Collector) and 1885 to 1930 for the boom in western Amazonia (Wasserstrom). EH.Net dates the shift to East Asian plantations from roughly 1910.

as_recorded.value: the first between 1879 and 1912 (known as the "rubber fever")

where.modern_name: Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil (one of two export centres; the boom covered the Amazon basin)
where.historical_name: Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil, with the rubber districts of Brazil, Bolivia and Peru

importance.justification: A commodity boom that built Amazon river cities and drove forced labour and violence against Indigenous people.

sources.title: The Horrors of "Rubber Fever" in the Amazon Rainforest
"Yo fuí vendida": Reconsidering Peonage and Genocide in Western Amazonia (Advances in Anthropology 7(2), doi:10.4236/aa.2017.72004)
sources.author: Robert Wasserstrom

reviewer_note: Least sure of the dates and the pin: pages disagree on the span (1879 to 1912 versus 1885 to 1930, and another page seen in searches says the boom ended in 1907), and the boom covered a whole basin, so the pin is Manaus with 1500 km uncertainty. The 13,000 Indians enslaved around 1904 is Wasserstrom's figure; no death toll is claimed. The Collector is a popular-history site (class other); EH.Net and Wasserstrom carry the claims on markets and labour.
